opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's something I think about a lot, because there's a real gap between an idea that looks great at small scale and one that actually holds up when you push it to hundreds of billions of parameters and trillions of tokens.

The first thing I look at is whether the gains are showing up as a better scaling curve, or just as a one-time bump at a single model size. A lot of architectural tweaks give you a nice improvement at, say, a hundred million parameters, and then the advantage shrinks as you scale up. Sometimes it disappears entirely, because the baseline Transformer was already learning whatever the tweak was helping with. So if a paper only reports one or two sizes, I'm pretty cautious. I'd much rather see three or four points along the curve with compute held fairly constant, so you can tell whether the lines are converging, staying parallel, or actually diverging in your favor.

The second thing is what I'd call systems friendliness. When we were training PaLM, a huge part of the work wasn't the modeling idea. It was making sure everything ran efficiently across thousands of accelerators. An architecture can look great in FLOPs on paper, but if it relies on operations that don't map well to the hardware, or it adds a lot of communication across devices, or it's numerically unstable in lower precision, then at scale you lose that advantage in wall-clock time and engineering pain. So I ask whether the idea is easy to shard, whether it keeps the matrix multiplies big and dense, and whether it introduces anything that might cause loss spikes over a long training run.

Third, I look at what they're evaluating. Perplexity improvements are a useful signal, but some of the most interesting capabilities, like multi-step reasoning or few-shot behavior, only really emerge at larger scales. So a small-scale result on perplexity doesn't always tell you how the model will do on the things you actually care about downstream.

And honestly, I don't want to discourage people who can't scale things themselves. Most academic labs simply don't have the compute, and a lot of important ideas started out as small experiments. What helps is when researchers are careful and honest. They should tune the baselines properly, report the compute budget, and be explicit about the regime they tested. That makes it much easier for those of us with bigger clusters to pick an idea up and decide whether it's worth a serious bet. The ideas that make it through tend to be simple, robust, and to improve the slope rather than just the intercept.

r001.rationale: It describes a real gap between small-scale promise and whether an architecture holds up at hundreds of billions of parameters and trillions of tokens.

r002.rationale: It evaluates scaling curves, hardware fit, stability, and downstream capabilities, showing that assessing an architecture requires judgment beyond simply applying a change.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing I'd say is that it's completely fair for a research group to publish an idea at small scale and not scale it themselves. Most groups don't have the compute to train at hundreds of billions of parameters, and the field would be poorer if we only heard from the handful of labs that do. So I don't hold it against the paper. But it does change how I read it.

What I'm looking for is whether the paper gives me the evidence to predict what happens at scale, rather than just a single result at one size. The most useful thing an architecture paper can do is show a scaling trend, even a modest one. If you train three or four models across an order of magnitude or two of compute and the gap over the baseline is holding or widening, that tells me something. If it's a single point comparison at, say, 300 million parameters, and the baseline is a Transformer that wasn't tuned very carefully, I've learned much less. A lot of architectural advantages in my experience are really compensating for a weakness that just disappears with more data and more parameters. The Transformer is a very strong baseline once you give it enough.

The second thing I look at is what the idea costs in systems terms. When we were scaling PaLM, a huge fraction of the work was about how the model maps onto the hardware. Things like whether an operation parallelizes cleanly across thousands of chips, whether it's memory bound, whether it breaks the nice dense matrix multiplications accelerators are good at. An architecture can look great on a FLOP count and be a disaster in wall clock time. So if a paper reports only FLOPs or only parameters and not throughput on real hardware, I treat the efficiency claims with some skepticism. Some of the most interesting ideas, like sparse attention variants or certain recurrent approaches, run into exactly this.

Then there's the question of whether the gains survive the rest of the recipe. At small scale you can get a few points on perplexity from a lot of things. But the things we actually care about in large models, like in-context learning, reasoning, instruction following, those emerge later and they're sensitive to data mixture, learning rate schedules, all of it. So I ask whether the idea is orthogonal to those knobs or whether it's going to interact with them in ways nobody has tested. Something like a different positional encoding or a normalization change is relatively easy to reason about. Something that changes the fundamental compute pattern is much harder.

And honestly, the last filter is a bit social. Does the idea have a simple story about why it should help more as you scale, not less? Mixture of experts is a good example. The argument for why it should keep paying off at scale is clean, you decouple parameter count from compute per token, and that argument held up when people actually did it. Ideas where the story is more "this inductive bias helps the model learn from limited data" tend to be exactly the ones that wash out, because the whole point of scaling is that you stop being limited by data in that way.

So when I see a promising architecture from a group that's leaving the scaling to others, I'm asking: did they show a trend, did they think about the hardware, is the gain likely to be independent of the rest of the training recipe, and is there a principled reason to believe it gets better rather than worse with scale. If a paper hits even two or three of those, it's worth someone spending real compute to find out. If it hits none of them, it's probably going to be one more idea that was true at a hundred million parameters and quietly disappeared.

r001.rationale: The response says small-scale results do not establish what will happen at scale and asks whether gains will hold or grow, expressing uncertainty about expected results.

r002.rationale: It describes judging scaling trends, hardware costs, interactions with the training recipe, and reasons gains might persist, showing that scaling requires more than mechanically applying an architecture change.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: what happens to the benefit as you scale? An architecture can look very promising at a small scale, but that doesn’t necessarily tell you whether the advantage will persist when you increase the parameters, the data, and the compute.

So I’d want to see a scaling trend across several sizes, with a strong baseline and comparable compute budgets. And I’d look at how efficiently it runs on the hardware. If an architecture needs fewer training steps but each step is much more expensive, that changes the comparison.

You don’t necessarily have to run the largest experiment to make a compelling case. But showing a consistent advantage across scales gives the next team a much better basis for deciding whether to invest in that larger experiment.

r001.rationale: The response says a small-scale advantage may not persist as parameters, data, and compute increase, directly identifying uncertainty about results at scale.

r002.rationale: It recommends comparing trends across scales and considering hardware efficiency, but does not characterize successfully scaling an architecture as requiring judgment beyond mechanically applying changes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: what happens as you scale? An architecture can look very promising at a smaller scale, but that doesn’t necessarily tell you how it will compare when you give it more compute, more data, and more parameters.

So I would want to see a scaling curve, even if it’s over a relatively modest range. Are you comparing against a well-tuned baseline at the same compute budget? Does the advantage persist as you increase the budget? And then there’s the systems question: can you implement it efficiently on the hardware you have? A theoretical reduction in computation doesn’t always translate into faster training.

You don’t need every research group to train the largest possible model. But evidence about how the approach scales makes it much easier to decide which ideas are worth taking to that next stage.

r001.rationale: It says an architecture that looks promising at smaller scale may not compare as well when given more compute, data, and parameters, directly expressing uncertainty about its results at scale.

r002.rationale: The response recommends evaluating scaling curves, baselines, and implementation efficiency, but does not characterize scaling as requiring judgment beyond mechanically applying changes.
